q: Two Go slices unexpectedly change together. Explain the likely cause.
a: Slices can refer to the same backing array. Copy elements when independent storage is required.
explanation: A slice has length and capacity in addition to its array reference. Appending may reuse capacity or allocate a new array, so sharing behavior depends on the operation and available capacity.
mistake: Treating every slice assignment as a deep copy.
followups: Can a small slice retain a large array?

q: A Go function returns an error interface containing a nil pointer, but err != nil. Why?
a: An interface can hold a dynamic type with a nil value. That interface is not the same as a nil interface.
explanation: Return a plain nil when there is no error. Trace both the dynamic type and stored value when debugging interface comparisons.
mistake: Assuming every interface containing nil compares equal to nil.

q: A cancelled HTTP request leaves Go workers running. How should the workers be designed?
a: Propagate context cancellation and make blocking operations select on cancellation or use context-aware APIs.
explanation: The owner should wait for worker completion and define who closes channels. Cancellation signals intent; it does not forcibly stop a goroutine. Release resources when returning.
mistake: Creating goroutines with no cancellation or completion path.
followups: Who should close the result channel?

q: Concurrent requests write to a shared Go map. How do you verify and fix the issue?
a: Run the race detector on exercised paths and use synchronization or a concurrency-safe ownership design.
explanation: Choose a mutex, an appropriate concurrent map, or single-owner access based on operations. A clean race run is useful evidence but only covers executions actually observed.
mistake: Assuming no detector warning proves all paths are race-free.
followups: How do you avoid holding a lock during I/O?

q: Design a bounded Go worker pool for batch requests.
a: Use a bounded queue, a fixed or controlled worker count, cancellation, and a clear result/error policy.
explanation: Specify ownership of input and output channels. Limit upstream admission as well as workers; otherwise pending work may still grow without bound. Test early cancellation and one failing task.
mistake: Launching one goroutine per item for an unbounded batch.
followups: How do you preserve input ordering?

q: A Go service spends too much time collecting garbage. What would you investigate?
a: Profile allocation and retained memory, then reduce measured temporary allocations or unnecessarily retained objects.
explanation: Inspect buffers, interface conversions, and collection growth with representative traffic. Pools can add complexity and retain memory; benchmark them rather than assuming they help.
mistake: Adding object pools everywhere before profiling.

q: How would you design shared Go packages without creating a tightly coupled platform?
a: Use small consumer-oriented interfaces, clear compatibility boundaries, and minimal dependencies.
explanation: Keep domain policy out of generic packages. Review error behavior, context ownership, and public types. Test real consumers before changes and document a versioning and deprecation policy.
mistake: Building one shared package that every service must import.

q: Design an ingestion service in Go that remains stable when a dependency slows down.
a: Bound admission, queueing, concurrency, and retries; propagate deadlines and expose saturation metrics.
explanation: Define accepted-work durability and retry identity. Protect the event loop of upstream systems by responding predictably under overload. Test degraded dependency behavior, not just peak healthy throughput.
mistake: Increasing goroutine counts until memory runs out.
